source_text: Sic nec de aliquibus insignibus. Caeterum satis inhumanum, si foeminae quidem per omnia viris subditae, honorigeram notam virginitatis suae praeferant, qua suspiciantur et circumspiciantur et magnificentur a fratribus, viri autem tot virgines, tot spadones voluntarii, caeco bono suo incedant, nihil gestantes, quod et ipsos faceret illustres. Debebunt etiam et ipsi aliqua sibi insignia defendere, aut pennas Garamantum, aut stropulos Barbarorum, aut cicadas Atheniensium, aut cirros Germanorum, aut stigmata Britonum: aut ex diverso fiat, capite velati in ecclesia lateant. Certi sumus Spiritum Sanctum magis masculis tale aliquid subscribere potuisse, si foeminis subscripsisset, cum praeter sexus auctoritatem, etiam ipsius continentiae nomine masculos potius honorari oportuisset; quorum quanto sexus avidior et calidior in foeminas, tanto continentia majoris ardoris laboratior, ideoque dignior omni ostentatione: si ostentatio, virginitatis est dignitas. Non enim et continentia virginitati antistat, sive viduorum, sive qui ex consensu contumeliam communem jam recusaverunt? Nam virginitas gratia constat, continentia vero virtute. Non concupiscendi, cui concupiscendo inoleveris, grande certamen est. Cujus autem concupiscendi ignoraveris fructum, facile non concupisces, adversarium non habens, concupiscentiam fructus. Quomodo ergo non magis viris aliquid tale Deus in honorem subscripsisset, vel quia familiariori, scilicet imagini suae, vel quia plus laboranti? Si autem nihil masculo, multo magis foeminae.
pass_a_gloss: Thus neither about some insignia. Moreover, it is sufficiently inhuman, if women indeed through all things subjected to men, may prefer a honorific note of their virginity, by which they are suspected and looked around and magnified by the brothers, but men, so many virgins, so many voluntary eunuchs, may proceed with blind good of their own, carrying nothing, which would also make them illustrious. They ought to also defend some insignia for themselves, or feathers of Garamantes, or strophions of Barbarians, or cicadas of Athenians, or hair of Germans, or stigmas of Britons: or on the other hand, veiled on the head, they may hide in the church. We are certain that the Holy Spirit could have more readily subscribed such a thing to men, if he had subscribed it to women, since beyond the authority of sex, the name of continence itself ought to have been more honored in men; whose sex is more eager and hotter towards women, so much more does continence labor with greater ardor, and is therefore more worthy of all display: if display is the dignity of virginity. For not even continence stands against virginity, whether of widows or of those who by consent have already refused common shame? For virginity consists of grace, but continence of virtue. Not to desire, to whom desiring you have grown accustomed, is a great struggle. But whose fruit of desire you have ignored, you will not easily desire, not having an adversary, the desire of the fruit. How then did God not subscribe such a thing more to men, either because they are more familiar, namely to his image, or because they labor more? But if nothing to the male, much more to the female.

pass_b_english: Let’s be clear: this isn't about a few badges. It is flatly inhumane that women, subjected to men in every respect, get to flaunt an honorific badge of their virginity—a badge that makes them suspects, spectacles, and celebrities among the brothers—while men, so many virgins, so many voluntary eunuchs, march on in their private virtue carrying nothing that would also make them illustrious. The men ought to defend some insignia for themselves too: Garamantian feathers, Barbarian strophiums, Athenian cicadas, German braids, British tattoos—or, failing that, let them veil their heads and hide in church. We are certain the Holy Spirit could have more readily authorized such a distinction for men, if he had authorized it for women; besides the authority of sex, the very name of continence ought to have been more honored in men, since their sex burns hotter and hungers more fiercely for women, their continence labors with greater ardor, and is therefore more worthy of all display—if display is virginity’s dignity. After all, continence does not outrank virginity, whether of widows or those who by mutual consent have already refused the common shame. Virginity consists in grace; continence consists in virtue. Not desiring, when you have grown accustomed to desiring, is a mighty struggle. But if you have never tasted the fruit of desire, you will not easily desire it, having no adversary—the desire for the fruit. How, then, did God not authorize such a distinction more for men, whether because they are more familiar to him—namely, his image—or because they labor more? But if nothing for the male, then much more for the female.
